name: Lai

catalog_citation: Melnik, Nurit. 1997. The sound system of Lai. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 20(2): 9-19.
catalog_locator: p. 16, section heading 'Stress'; Conclusion p. 19 (pp. 8 and 11)
catalog_quote: It appears that Lai treats the syllable final position on a par with the word final position. This may be a consequence of the morphology of Lai. A majority of the polysyllabic words in my lexicon are compound words, where each syllable is a word. Stress Stress in Lai falls invariably on the last syllable. [Conclusion, p. 19] In this paper I have attempted to describe the sound system of Lai by providing an inventory of the phonemes and allophones of the language, including their distribution. Additionally, I discussed a number of its interesting phonetic characteristics: ... •an undeviating stress pattern

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word, with no exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: based on a ~300-word lexicon elicited from one speaker (Kenneth VanBik, born and raised in Haka, Chin State) plus STEDT data; the author notes most polysyllabic words in her lexicon are compounds of monosyllabic words. One-sentence statement with no examples or instrumental support. The language is tonal: Hyman & VanBik (2002, 2004) describe a three-way tone contrast on largely monosyllabic words and phrase-level 'left-prominence', and do not mention word stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Melnik 1997 describes the Lai of Haka (Hakha) town, Chin State, Myanmar, from a single Haka-born consultant (Kenneth VanBik); this is the Hakha Lai variety = haka1240 itself, not a divergent dialect. Newland 1897 calls the same variety the 'Baungshe dialect'. Lalremzami 2013 (unread) covers Haka and Khuafo varieties spoken in Mizoram, India.

new_statements.quote: 4.9. Suprasegmental Phonology[17]: Suprasegmental is a term used in phonetics and phonology to refer to a vocal effect which extends over more than one sound segment in an utterance. Length and Tone of Lai are discussed under suprasegmental phonology. Tone function as a means of differentiating lexical items. [...] [fn. 17:] Pitch and stress is not included under suprasegmental phonology because as they do not affect the logical semantics interpretation of an utterance. [...] [4.9.2, p. 86:] In Lai language, tones are phonemic and it has contrastive lexical items. There are four tones in Lai namely, two register tones (high and low) and two contour tones (falling and rising).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's final-stress record (Melnik 1997: 'Stress in Lai falls invariably on the last syllable'): an invariable placement is by definition non-contrastive, which is all Lalremzami asserts. It adds no placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts 'final'; what it adds is that the Mizoram Thantlang variety is tonal with four tones (vs. Melnik's and Hyman & VanBik's three for Hakha) and that the author regards stress as semantically irrelevant. Describes the Thantlang (Thlantlang) variety of Lai spoken in Lawngtlai District, Mizoram, India, a dialect of Hakha Lai (haka1240), not the Hakha variety of Chin State.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis treats Thantlang Lai as a tone language (four lexical tones H, L, F, R; phonemic vowel length in closed syllables) and deliberately leaves stress out of the description on the ground that stress does not affect meaning, i.e. stress is non-contrastive. It gives NO statement of where stress falls. The only other uses of 'stress' are a textbook definition of falling/rising diphthongs (p. 69) and literature-review prose.
new_statements.exceptions: none; stress is excluded from the scope of the description (sec. 1.6, p. 13: 'Pitch and stress is not included under suprasegmental phonology as they do not affect the logical semantics interpretation of an utterance').
new_statements.identity_note: Lalremzami 2013 describes the Thantlang (Thlantlang) variety of Lai as spoken in Lawngtlai District, Mizoram, India (ch. 1, p. 1: 'In Mizoram, there are two varieties of Lai i.e. Thantlang and Khuafo. The present study described only Thantlang variety'), with internal dialectal variation noted in sec. 4.4.4; the author equates Lai with 'Haka-Chin' and contrasts her data with Peterson's Hakha Chin of Myanmar. Melnik 1997 and Hyman & VanBik describe Hakha Lai proper. Both fall under haka1240.
